links.took: Sierra's 256-color VGA icon-driven point-and-click interface and fairy-tale royal adventure structure.
links.added: Introduced branching endgame paths, nuanced puzzles co-designed by Jane Jensen, and richer literary world-building across the Land of the Green Isles.
links.extra: Co-designed by Roberta Williams and Jane Jensen, it became Sierra's most acclaimed classic adventure.

links.took: Jane Jensen's research-heavy folklore plotting, layered character dialogue, and branching literary puzzle design at Sierra.
links.added: Shifted from fairy-tale royalty to a gritty New Orleans supernatural detective thriller with day-by-day investigation chapters.

src.t: Wikipedia: Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers

links.extra: Sierra greenlit Jensen's original Gabriel Knight concept directly off the critical triumph of her work on King's Quest VI.

links.took: Arcade light-gun wave shooting where players pick off popping-out threats while sparing innocent hostages.
links.added: Replaced hand-drawn military sprites with digitized live-action crime scenes and off-screen revolver reloading using Konami's Justifier gun.
links.extra: Its photorealistic digitized violence drew 1993 U.S. Senate hearings alongside Night Trap and Mortal Kombat.

links.took: High-stakes arcade police shootouts with civilian rescue penalties and timed enemy threat escalation.
links.added: Rebuilt the urban cop light-gun fantasy in 3D Sega Model 2 polygons with color-coded countdown lock-on reticles and locational hit reactions.
links.extra: Konami's 1992 arcade hit proved modern urban police themes could dominate light-gun cabinets.

links.took: High-speed illegal highway motorcycle racing mixed with close-quarters punching, kicking, and club swinging.
links.added: Added two-player split-screen multiplayer, nitro-equipped superbikes, steel chains, and aggressive patrolling police officers.
links.extra: Expanded Electronic Arts' Genesis hit across five distinct American road circuits from Hawaii to Alaska.

links.took: Sega's lushly animated 16-bit Disney fairy-tale platforming built around gentle pacing and storybook set-pieces.
links.added: Introduced simultaneous two-player co-op with Mickey and Donald pulling each other up ledges, magic-cape attacks, and character-exclusive routes.
links.extra: Developed internally at Sega as the direct Genesis successor to Castle of Illusion.

links.took: Konami's accessible licensed-cartoon arcade beat 'em up combat with simple attacks and drop-in multiplayer spectacle.
links.added: Scaled the cabinet to an unprecedented dual-screen six-player marquee with health-draining Mutant Power screen-clearing specials.
links.extra: Konami's six-player deluxe cabinet became one of the most recognizable centerpieces of 1990s arcades.

links.took: Capcom's CPS-1 belt-scrolling street brawling, chunky grab-and-throw combat, and crowd-control super moves.
links.added: Added three-player simultaneous co-op, sprint-dash strikes, reloadable firearms, wild dinosaurs, and a playable Cadillac driving stage.
links.extra: Adapted Mark Schultz's Xenozoic Tales comic into one of Capcom's fastest and most varied CPS-1 brawlers.

links.took: Apogee's episodic PC shareware distribution and smooth-scrolling side-view sci-fi platforming.
links.added: Cranked up run-and-gun action with 256-color VGA parallax art, rapid-fire upgradeable blasters, destructible scenery, and a wisecracking action hero.
links.extra: Created by Todd Replogle and Allen Blum at Apogee Software as the 2D peak of Duke's pre-3D era.

links.took: Apogee's irreverent alien-blasting action hero, episodic shareware structure, and rapid-fire sci-fi weapons.
links.added: Vaulted the character into Ken Silverman's 3D Build Engine with interactive urban levels, voiced one-liners, and satirical pop-culture parodies.
links.extra: Bridged Apogee's classic 2D shareware catalog directly into 3D Realms' blockbuster 1996 FPS.

links.took: Isometric free-roaming attack-helicopter missions balancing fuel, armor, ammo pickups, and winch rescues.
links.added: Introduced switchable vehicles—hovercraft, F-117 stealth fighter, and motorcycle—plus night-vision ops and Washington, D.C. defenses.
links.extra: Second entry in EA's Strike series, expanding its tactical sandbox far beyond desert gunship runs.

links.took: Rotoscoped ledge-climbing acrobatics, lethal trap timing, and tense blade-to-blade dueling under a ticking clock.
links.added: Expanded the setting into lush VGA rooftops, ruined temples, and flying carpets while adding multi-enemy swordfights and out-of-body shadow powers.

src.t: Wikipedia: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame

links.extra: Supervised by Jordan Mechner at Brøderbund, deepening the series' Arabian Nights mythology.

links.took: Lori and Corey Cole's hybrid point-and-click adventure and stat-building RPG allowing imported characters to solve quests by class.
links.added: Brought the formula into gothic Slavic folklore with voiced narration by John Rhys-Davies, day-night curses, and icon-driven VGA exploration.

src.t: Wikipedia: Quest for Glory: Shadows of Darkness

links.extra: Widely celebrated as the atmospheric and narrative peak of Sierra's Quest for Glory saga.

links.took: Director Nobuya Nakazato's relentless multi-phase boss choreography and kinetic mid-stage set-pieces at Konami.
links.added: Channeled that intensity into a Mega Drive mascot action-platformer built around Sparkster's charge-up directional jetpack dash and wall bounces.
links.extra: Nakazato led Konami's Sega Genesis debut for Sparkster immediately after directing Contra III on SNES.

links.took: Grid-based Japanese tactical RPG skirmishes paired with explorable towns and animated close-up battle cutaways.
links.added: Replaced segmented chapters with a seamless free-roaming overworld, hidden promotion items, branching class upgrades, and larger tactical maps.
links.extra: Developed by Sonic! Software Planning (later Camelot) as the signature 16-bit Genesis strategy RPG.

links.took: Joe Musashi's deliberate shuriken throwing, double-jump somersaults, and four-element Ninjitsu magic on Mega Drive.
links.added: Transformed combat fluidity with sprinting slashes, aerial dive kicks, wall jumps, sword blocking, and high-speed horseback and surfboard stages.

src.t: Wikipedia: Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master

links.extra: Delayed and reworked by Sega until it achieved one of the crispest 16-bit action-platformer movement sets.

links.took: Pre-rendered full-motion video presentation turning interactive cinema into timed reflex sequences.
links.added: Replaced discrete button prompts with analog cursor aiming, cockpit rail-shooting, and trench runs that helped drive early PC CD-ROM adoption.
links.extra: LucasArts' 1993 CD-ROM blockbuster sold over 1.5 million copies and served as a killer app for optical drives.

links.took: First-person TIE Fighter interception, asteroid dodging, and the culminating Death Star trench run.
links.added: Reimagined Atari's vector-wireframe movie set-pieces using streaming 3D-rendered CD-ROM video, John Williams audio, and ground blaster stages.
links.extra: Directed by Vince Lee at LucasArts as a multimedia showpiece for the CD-ROM era.

links.took: Capcom's six-button special-move fighting framework and twelve-fighter World Warrior roster.
links.added: Debuted Capcom's CPS-2 arcade board, an onscreen combo counter, eight-player tournament networking, and four iconic newcomers including Cammy and Fei Long.
links.extra: First game built on Capcom's CPS-2 hardware, laying the visual and roster groundwork for Super Turbo.

links.took: The expanded sixteen-character CPS-2 roster, reworked hit-stun animations, and combo-tracking foundation.
links.added: Introduced the Super Combo meter, air combos, tech throws, adjustable turbo speed, and secret boss Akuma.

src.t: Wikipedia: Super Street Fighter II Turbo

links.extra: Directly iterated on The New Challengers within five months to create the enduring competitive standard.

links.took: Sun-soaked cross-country arcade road-trip checkpoints, traffic weaving, and exuberant convertible flair.
links.added: Translated the coast-to-coast highway sprint into Midway's texture-mapped 3D polygonal V-Unit hardware with double-tap wheelie boosts and landmark shortcuts.
links.extra: Designed by Eugene Jarvis's team at Midway and famously promoted as a centerpiece for Nintendo's Ultra 64.

links.took: Treasure's multi-jointed Genesis sprite bosses, relentless visual gags, and inventive genre-twisting set-pieces.
links.added: Swapped twin-weapon run-and-gun shooting for a stage-play puppet platformer centered on launching and swapping 18 distinct power-up heads.
links.extra: Directed by Hiroshi Iuchi at Treasure, showcasing their knack for surreal 16-bit hardware tricks.

links.took: Quarter-circle special moves, projectile zoning, and competitive one-on-one 2D fighting pacing.
links.added: Tailored arcade fighting for DOS PCs with giant HAR combat robots, interactive arena hazards, and a persistent prize-money tournament upgrade career.
links.extra: Built by Rob Elam's Diversions Entertainment and published by Epic MegaGames as a landmark PC shareware fighter.

links.took: Accessible hex-grid combined-arms tactics where terrain, supply, and unit matchups govern quick turn-based battles.
links.added: Added a persistent core WWII army that gains veteran experience and upgrades across branching historical and what-if operational campaigns.
links.extra: Strategic Simulations' 1994 breakout launched the Five Star General line and brought hex wargaming to a mass PC audience.

links.took: Proved deep, historically grounded WWII operational strategy with branching alternate-history theaters could thrive on mainstream PCs.
links.added: Expanded theater-level hex battles into a global continuous-time grand strategy simulation spanning diplomacy, industry, research, and supply chains.
links.extra: Panzer General reshaped commercial PC wargaming expectations throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s.

links.took: Instantaneous light-gun target-gallery shooting where split-second aim determines score.
links.added: Packed dozens of rapid-fire comic precision, speed, and memory micro-challenges into a competitive two-player arcade party format.
links.extra: Released as Gun Bullet in Japan by Namco, turning light-gun shooting into a beloved arcade party staple.

links.took: Rapid-fire, five-second comic arcade micro-challenges that explain their rules in a single blunt imperative.
links.added: Distilled that rapid-cut rhythm onto Game Boy Advance D-pad and single-button inputs with escalating speed-ups and absurd surrealist vignettes.
links.extra: Game historians routinely cite Point Blank and Bishi Bashi as key arcade precursors to WarioWare's microgame loop.

links.took: Relentless vertical-scrolling fighter-jet shooting over industrial and military ground installations.
links.added: Brought arcade-grade VGA scrolling to DOS shareware with an inter-mission hangar shop for buying shields, lasers, and screen-clearing megabombs.

src.t: Wikipedia: Raptor: Call of the Shadows

links.extra: Developed by Scott Host's Cygnus Studios and published by Apogee Software in 1994.

links.took: The DOS shareware vertical shoot 'em up formula built around earning credits from downed enemies to upgrade ship hardware between stages.
links.added: Deepened between-stage ship customization with mix-and-match front, rear, and sidekick weapons, generator power management, and lore datastores.
links.extra: Together, Raptor and Tyrian defined the golden era of mid-1990s PC shareware shoot 'em ups.

links.took: Sonic Team's vibrant Mega Drive platforming craft and the original scrapped pre-Sonic rabbit concept centered on grabbing objects with stretchable limbs.
links.added: Replaced blazing spin-dash speed with eight-directional stretchy-arm grabbing, headbutt slingshots, pole-swinging, and environmental puzzle platforming.

src.t: Yuji Naka & Sonic Team interviews on Feel / Ristar prototype; Wikipedia: Ristar

links.extra: Yuji Naka documented that Sonic began as a grab-focused rabbit prototype whose discarded mechanics were later revived for Ristar.

links.took: Sega's hard-hitting 16-bit urban beat 'em up combat, Yuzo Koshiro's club electronics, and distinct character move kits.
links.added: Introduced universal sprinting, vertical dodge rolls, a recharging special-attack gauge, weapon-specific blitzes, and branching endings.
links.extra: Released as Bare Knuckle III in Japan, pushing Genesis beat 'em up speed and mechanics to their 16-bit limit.

links.took: Fast-paced urban brawler move kits, unlockable roster variants, and risky crowd-control special-attack timing.
links.added: Paired hand-drawn HD animation with recoverable green-health special spending and wall-bounce juggles while preserving unlockable Streets of Rage 3 characters with full dash-and-roll mobility.
links.extra: Dotemu, Lizardcube, and Guard Crush directly honored all three 16-bit games' move-set distinctions.

links.took: Pattern-reading boss boxing duels built around telegraphing enemy tells, crisp dodges, and rapid counterpunches.
links.added: Restored the arcade cabinet's translucent fighter silhouette on SNES alongside a rapid-fire Super Punch meter and dizzy combo knockouts.
links.extra: Developed by Nintendo IRD under Genyo Takeda, blending NES accessibility with arcade visual clarity.

links.took: Capcom's six-button 2D fighting engine, special-move command inputs, and tight arcade footsies.
links.added: Launched Capcom's hyper-fighter era with towering Super Jumps, multi-hit aerial combos, rolling ukemi recoveries, and multi-tiered X-Power super gauges.

src.t: Wikipedia: X-Men: Children of the Atom (video game)

links.extra: Capcom's first Marvel fighting game on CPS-2, introducing Akuma as a hidden guest character.

links.took: Large hand-animated Marvel sprites, vertical Super Jumps, air-combo physics, and screen-filling Hyper Combos.
links.added: Paired the X-Men directly against Street Fighter icons in two-on-two tag-team bouts with switch-out health recovery and dual Variable Combinations.
links.extra: Directly carried over Children of the Atom's sprites and aerial-rave engine to launch the entire Capcom Vs. subgenre.

links.took: Polygonal 3D arena fighting with ring-out boundaries and dynamic camera framing.
links.added: Introduced dedicated shoulder-button 3D sidestep rolls, medieval weapons, and 2D-style projectile specials as an early PlayStation showcase.
links.extra: Tamsoft's January 1995 release helped convince Western players that PlayStation could bring 3D arcade fighters home.

links.took: Proved mainstream 3D console audiences loved weapon-wielding polygonal fighters with lateral 3D evasion.
links.added: Replaced sluggish fireball zoning with Namco's crisp horizontal-and-vertical slash geometry, Guard Impacts, and smooth 8-way sidestepping.
links.extra: Soul Edge debuted in arcades in December 1995 as 3D weapon fighting rapidly matured beyond Toshinden.

links.took: Origin Systems' detailed interactive isometric world engine evolved through Ultima VII and Ultima VIII.
links.added: Rebuilt that RPG tech under programmer Tony Zurovec into an explosive sci-fi tactical action shooter featuring destructible cover, rolling acrobatics, and live-action FMV briefings.
links.extra: Built on an overhauled Ultima VIII: Pagan engine by Origin's Loose Cannon Productions group.

links.took: Dystopian corporate-state cyberpunk aesthetics and high-lethality isometric urban firefights.
links.added: Zoomed from four-agent squad command down to direct single-commando keyboard control with security-camera hacking and heavily destructible rooms.
links.extra: Combined Bullfrog-style cyberpunk tone with Origin's rich environmental interactivity.

links.took: Yuji Horii's sweeping Zenithia-trilogy storytelling, wagon party swapping, and brisk SNES turn-based battles.
links.added: Intertwined parallel Real and Dream overworlds with an expansive job-vocation mastery system allowing hybrid advanced classes.
links.extra: First mainline Dragon Quest developed by Heartbeat, concluding the Zenithia trilogy on Super Famicom.

links.took: Sega AM2's 60fps Model 2 3D martial-arts engine and three-button Punch, Kick, Guard core.
links.added: Replaced open ring-outs with walled chain-link cages for rebound combos and introduced breakable body armor that raises damage taken when shattered.
links.extra: Directed by Hiroshi Kataoka under Yu Suzuki's AM2 division with youthful street-fashion designs.

links.took: Kirby's signature inhale-and-copy ability mechanics brought back onto the monochrome Game Boy.
links.added: Introduced three rideable Animal Friends—Rick, Kine, and Coo—that mutate each Copy Ability into unique elemental and traversal attacks.
links.extra: Directed by Shinichi Shimomura at HAL Laboratory, kicking off the recurring Dark Matter trilogy.

links.took: Bungie's computer-terminal sci-fi storytelling, ambient sound design, and sleek Mac first-person gunplay.
links.added: Expanded onto sunlit alien ruins on Lh'owon with swimming physics, dual-wielded lever-action shotguns, and cooperative campaign play.
links.extra: Released on Mac and Windows 95, cementing Bungie's narrative ambition and multiplayer craftsmanship.

links.took: Bungie's trademark rampant-AI lore, alien coalition battles, motion-tracker radar, and punchy sci-fi sandbox combat.
links.added: Brought Bungie's sci-fi universe into expansive 3D outdoor vehicle sandboxes with regenerating shields, dual-stick console aiming, and seamless grenade throws.

src.t: Wikipedia: Marathon 2: Durandal; Halo: Combat Evolved

links.extra: Jason Jones and Bungie carried recurring symbols, AI rampancy themes, and combat cadence straight from Durandal into Halo.

links.took: Mid-1990s Sega CD full-motion-video novelty and moral-panic debates over video game realism.
links.added: Subverted FMV gimmicks into an unreleased prank anthology featuring the infamous Desert Bus—an eight-hour, 45-mph real-time highway drive that drifts slightly right.

src.t: Wikipedia: Penn & Teller's Smoke and Mirrors

links.extra: Shelved when Absolute Entertainment folded in 1995, Desert Bus later spawned the multi-million-dollar Desert Bus for Hope charity marathon.

links.took: Desert Bus's deadpan embrace of grueling, deliberately unrewarding endurance as conceptual dark comedy.
links.added: Turned punishing frustration into a precision hammer-climbing physics climb paired with philosophical developer commentary on failure and persistence.

src.t: Wikipedia: Penn & Teller's Smoke and Mirrors

links.extra: Desert Bus became the foundational touchstone for modern anti-fun endurance games and charity streaming marathons.

links.took: Ron Gilbert's SCUMM point-and-click adventure engine, hotspot interactivity, and comic inventory puzzles.
links.added: Removed text verb bars entirely for a single-click, screen-filling animated cartoon playground built for young children with randomized puzzle variations.
links.extra: Ron Gilbert co-founded Humongous Entertainment after LucasArts, powering Putt-Putt with an evolved SCUMM engine.

links.took: Capcom's Super Combo gauge, rapid CPS-2 tempo, and high-stakes 2D fighting footsies.
links.added: Introduced three-tier Super meters, defensive Alpha Counters, air blocking, Chain Combos, and bold anime-styled sprite animation.
links.extra: Canonically bridged Street Fighter I and II while bringing Final Fight's Guy and Sodom into the roster.

links.took: Dial-a-combo chains, the Run button, multi-tiered stages, and high-speed digitized 2D arcade kombat.
links.added: Restored absent fan-favorite ninjas like Scorpion, Kitana, and Reptile while adding 2-on-2 bouts, 8-player tournaments, and refined competitive balance.
links.extra: Quickly superseded vanilla MK3 in arcades to become the enduring competitive pinnacle of 2D Mortal Kombat.

links.took: Gunpei Yokoi's R&D1 shoulder-bashing treasure hunt, power-up hats, and weighty antihero platforming.
links.added: Exploited the Virtual Boy's stereoscopic red-LED optics so Wario leaps seamlessly between foreground and deep-background dungeon planes.
links.extra: Widely acclaimed as the finest game released on Nintendo's short-lived Virtual Boy hardware.

links.took: Two-plane side-scrolling level design where characters launch back and forth between foreground and background paths to dodge hazards and find secrets.
links.added: Rendered multi-plane barrel-cannon leaps in vibrant full-color 3D Wii vistas with collapsing background structures and timed silhouette runs.
links.extra: Retro Studios later popularized foreground-to-background stage interplay first mastered by R&D1 on Virtual Boy.

links.took: Sega's 60fps Model 2 3D arcade arena geometry and tense one-on-one competitive spacing.
links.added: Fused fighting-game mind games with blazingly fast twin-stick mecha shooting, dash-canceling, and lock-on beam volleys designed by Hajime Katoki.
links.extra: Directed by Juro Watari at Sega AM3, pioneering modern high-speed 3D arena mecha combat.

links.took: Real-time strategic world-map army movement paired with semi-automated squad clashes led by named heroes.
links.added: Scaled tactical encounters on Sega Saturn up to 100-vs-100 sprite armies executing live formation charges and general spells across eight playable monarchs.
links.extra: Developed by J-Force and Sega, becoming one of the Saturn's most celebrated strategy-RPG exclusives.

links.took: The thrilling split between strategic castle-map conquest and real-time massed battlefield formation clashes.
links.added: Moved both strategic campaign diplomacy and thousands-strong tactical armies into realistic 3D PC feudal Japanese warfare with morale and terrain elevation.
links.extra: Dragon Force showcased massed real-time formation spectacles on console years before Total War perfected the hybrid on PC.

links.took: Brisk 3D polygonal arcade handling, vibrant blue-sky speed, and exhilarating drift corners.
links.added: Turned steep San Francisco streets into stunt playgrounds packed with towering air jumps, hidden shortcut tunnels, and dramatic car-wrecking crashes.

src.t: Wikipedia: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing

links.extra: Atari Games' 1996 arcade hit spawned a beloved N64 stunt-racing trilogy.

links.took: High-speed urban arcade racing where reckless shortcut driving and bone-crunching collisions sit front and center.
links.added: Tied oncoming traffic near-misses directly to a refillable boost gauge and showcased cinematic multi-car slow-motion pileups.

src.t: Wikipedia: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing

links.extra: Rush's gleeful stunt physics and explosive wrecks helped shift arcade racing beyond clean circuit laps.

links.took: Hudson Soft's grid-based bomb-trapping couch battles, power-up pickups, and sudden-death closing walls.
links.added: Expanded local multiplayer to an extraordinary ten players simultaneously on one giant scrolling arena via dual Sega Saturn multitaps.
links.extra: Remains widely regarded as the high-water mark of classic 2D multiplayer Bomberman.

links.took: LucasArts' Expanded Universe Star Wars action storytelling and multi-weapon sci-fi firefights.
links.added: Blended third-person 3D N64 blaster exploration with an iconic opening Battle of Hoth snowspeeder flight, Mos Eisley swoop chases, and space combat.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire (video game)

links.extra: Anchor video game of Lucasfilm's 1996 multimedia event bridging The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi.

links.took: Creator Doug TenNapel's offbeat cartoon humor, rubbery physical comedy, and idiosyncratic character design.
links.added: Moved into a hand-sculpted stop-motion claymation world built from three tons of clay, turning surreal sight gags into an exploratory adventure.
links.extra: TenNapel left Shiny Entertainment to direct The Neverhood for DreamWorks Interactive with Terry S. Taylor's jazz soundtrack.

links.took: Solitary point-and-click island exploration through cryptic contraptions, wordless environmental clues, and pre-rendered first-person transitions.
links.added: Replaced solemn photo-rendered mystery with slapstick stop-motion claymation, third-person movement rooms, and a famously absurd 38-screen lore hallway.
links.extra: Demonstrated how Myst's quiet puzzle-world format could carry tactile physical comedy.

links.took: Ensemble 16-bit Japanese RPG storytelling with character-specific skill identities and sweeping emotional set-pieces.
links.added: Blended vibrant 2D top-down towns and Zelda-like character dungeon Tools with full 3D PlayStation polygonal turn-based battles in a sci-fi Wild West.
links.extra: Developed by Media.Vision as one of the earliest original RPG pillars for the Sony PlayStation.

links.took: Real-time battlefield unit command, tank skirmishes, and mouse-driven squad tactics.
links.added: Eliminated base-building and resource harvesting entirely, forcing players to race for territorial sector flags that automatically speed up robot factory output.
links.extra: The Bitmap Brothers' frantic 1996 RTS pioneered pure territory-capture economics.

links.took: Flag-based territorial sector control replacing passive mineral harvesting to force constant frontline skirmishes.
links.added: Expanded capture-point economies with squad-based cover, morale suppression, and upgradable listening posts in Relic's grimdark Warhammer 40,000 RTS.

src.t: Wikipedia: Z (video game); Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War

links.extra: Z's flag-capture economy laid the conceptual blueprint for Relic's celebrated territorial RTS era.

links.took: Dividing maps into capturable territory sectors whose ownership directly fuels wartime production instead of worker mining.
links.added: Tied linked sector supply chains to Manpower, Munitions, and Fuel while adding destructible WWII cover and directional suppression fire.

src.t: Wikipedia: Z (video game); Company of Heroes

links.extra: Historians trace Relic's landmark territorial-control loop directly back to The Bitmap Brothers' Z.

links.took: Rare's knack for bold visual polish, tight medal-chasing replayability, and inventive Nintendo hardware design.
links.added: Pivoted into a 3D N64 demolition puzzle-action original where players pilot bulldozers, dump trucks, and mechs to raze buildings ahead of a runaway nuclear missile carrier.
links.extra: Rare's first Nintendo 64 release, conceived by a tiny team led by Martin Wakeley before GoldenEye 007.

links.took: Visible battlefield positioning, dynamic camera framing, and time-driven active turn-based JRPG flow.
links.added: Introduced the shared IP Gauge timeline where timing Critical strikes cancels enemy spell casts mid-windup and knocks foes back along the turn bar.
links.extra: Game Arts' Saturn classic created one of the most revered active turn-based battle systems in JRPG history.

links.took: Making turn order explicitly visible and manipulable so players plan delays, haste, and interrupts tactically.
links.added: Refined visible turn queues into the fully deterministic Conditional Turn-Based (CTB) sidebar with instant mid-battle party swapping.

src.t: Wikipedia: Grandia (video game); Final Fantasy X

links.extra: Grandia's timeline clarity influenced a generation of turn-order-visible JRPG combat designs.

links.took: Activision's 3D vehicle-simulation engine, directional armor diagrams, and cockpit weapon-group management.
links.added: Rebuilt that sim tech for roof-turret 1970s muscle-car highway combat steeped in funk music, poetry, and alternate-history oil-crisis storytelling.
links.extra: Directed by Zack Norman at Activision directly atop the MechWarrior 2 engine.

links.took: Weaponized vehicular destruction featuring machine guns, rockets, mines, and distinct car archetypes.
links.added: Paired vehicular combat with realistic suspension physics, salvageable chassis parts, and an episodic blaxploitation story campaign across the American Southwest.
links.extra: Bridged console arena car-combat thrills with PC simulation depth.

links.took: Curved 2.5D movement tracks weaving through colorful 3D environments with sweeping perspective camera swings.
links.added: Built traditional tactile platforming around 2D sprites in rotating 3D spaces, anchored by a Wind Bullet ring that inflates enemies for double-jumps and foreground-to-background throws.
links.extra: Directed by Hideo Yoshizawa at Namco, setting the visual and mechanical template for 2.5D console platformers.

links.took: Playful open-ended 3D toybox exploration where players freely roam an island hub triggering standalone activities.
links.added: Brought the LEGO brick license into its first 3D open-world PC sandbox with five switchable minifigures, custom-built vehicles, and the Brickster chase.
links.extra: Developed by Mindscape, proving LEGO playsets could thrive as interactive 3D digital worlds.

links.took: Irreverent minifigure slapstick, brick-built vehicles, and lighthearted family-friendly 3D LEGO exploration.
links.added: Married LEGO comedy to Traveller's Tales' drop-in two-player action-platforming, stud-collecting, and wordless cinematic movie parodies.

src.t: Wikipedia: Lego Island; Lego Star Wars: The Video Game

links.extra: LEGO Island launched the modern era of 3D LEGO games that Traveller's Tales later turned into a juggernaut.

links.took: Shiny Entertainment's offbeat visual surrealism, kinetic humor, and razor-sharp action pacing under David Perry and Nick Bruty.
links.added: Pushed into early 3D third-person PC action with a pioneering zoomed sniper-helmet mode, reusable ribbon parachute gliding, and towering alien minecrawlers.
links.extra: Its instant switch from third-person running to first-person zoomed sniping anticipated modern shooter optics.

links.took: Two-on-two Marvel-and-Capcom tag-team hyper fighting, aerial raves, and crossover super combos.
links.added: Introduced the dedicated Variable Assist button to summon a benched partner for an attack without tagging out—defining modern tag-fighter neutral play.

src.t: Wikipedia: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter

links.extra: Invented the quick partner-assist mechanic that became foundational across Marvel vs. Capcom 2, Skullgirls, and Dragon Ball FighterZ.

links.took: Hyper-speed two-on-two Marvel tag combat and mid-combo partner assist calls.
links.added: Opened the Capcom side beyond Street Fighter to Mega Man, Morrigan, Strider Hiryu, and Captain Commando alongside randomized Guest Assist partners.

src.t: Wikipedia: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes

links.extra: Direct arcade link between Capcom's Street Fighter crossover entries and its broader company-wide Vs. series.

links.took: Wall-kicking, dashing, armor capsules, and eight-Maverick stage selection from Capcom's futuristic Mega Man reboot.
links.added: Elevated the subseries to 32-bit hardware with lush animated cutscenes and a full, distinct melee-only campaign playing as Z-Saber-wielding Zero.
links.extra: Widely acclaimed as the peak 32-bit entry in the Mega Man X subseries.

links.took: 3D Realms' interactive Build Engine levels, destructible props, secret hunting, and brash action-movie parody.
links.added: Pushed Ken Silverman's engine further with true room-over-room 3D bridges, drivable tanks and boats, transparent water, and close-range katana slicing.
links.extra: Alongside Duke Nukem 3D and Blood, it formed the iconic trio of 1990s Build Engine shooters.

links.took: Julian Gollop's squad-level alien-defense tactics, destructible terrain, and strategic base-and-research management.
links.added: Focused the war inside a single living futuristic mega-city with competing corporate factions, destructible skyscrapers, and toggleable real-time or turn-based combat.
links.extra: Marked Julian Gollop and Mythos Games' ambitious direct return to the series after Terror from the Deep.

links.took: Julian Gollop's multi-faction geopolitical maneuvering—where rival human syndicates can be allied with, raided, or alienated during an alien crisis.
links.added: Modernized those competing human-faction dilemmas with free-aim ballistic targeting, mutating Pandoran enemies, and global Geoscape havens.
links.extra: Gollop's Snapshot Games explicitly drew on his 1990s X-COM designs, including Apocalypse's rival faction politics.

links.took: Nintendo EAD's tactile N64 surface-physics simulation and analog weight-shifting carved through dynamic terrain.
links.added: Translated water-buoyancy feel onto powdery, icy, and packed snow slopes with responsive trick-landing balance and realistic board-edge carving.
links.extra: Programmed by Giles Goddard and Colin Reed at Nintendo EAD as an N64 extreme-sports technical milestone.

links.took: Proved 3D console snowboarding could marry responsive analog carving with rhythmic jump-trick flow.
links.added: Cranked alpine runs into exaggerated PlayStation 2 arcade spectacle with towering fantasy tracks, mid-air uber-tricks, and turbo boost gauges.
links.extra: 1080° set the technical snowboarding benchmark that EA Canada's SSX subsequently blew open into arcade excess.

links.took: Quiet, first-person wandering through surreal, uncanny architectural spaces divorced from arcade combat.
links.added: Stripped away even puzzles, scores, and objectives—adapting designer Hiroko Nishikawa's ten-year dream journal so touching any wall or figure warps players into shifting psychedelic dreamscapes.
links.extra: Created by Japanese multimedia artist Osamu Sato at OutSide Directors Company for PlayStation in 1998.

links.took: Scoreless, goal-free exploration of haunting, associative dreamscapes governed by surreal dream logic rather than victory states.
links.added: Reimagined aimless dream wandering in top-down RPG Maker 2003 pixel art as Madotsuki explores interconnected nexus doors collecting eerie Effects.

src.t: Wikipedia: LSD: Dream Emulator; Yume Nikki

links.extra: Both Japanese cult landmarks became twin foundational pillars of the modern surreal exploration and walking-sim indie scene.

links.took: Isometric graphical MMORPG persistence, player-driven PvP conflict, and shared-world clan economics.
links.added: Tailored persistent-world warfare for South Korea's booming PC bang cafes with streamlined click combat and massive Blood Pledge castle-siege tax wars.
links.extra: Led by Jake Song at NCSoft, Lineage became one of the highest-grossing and most influential MMOs in Asian gaming history.

links.took: Brisk mouse-click isometric hack-and-slash combat, dark medieval gothic art, and instant potion-chugging feedback.
links.added: Expanded click-driven dark-fantasy dungeon grinding into a massively multiplayer online kingdom ruled by warring player guilds.
links.extra: Its snappy Diablo-like accessibility made it an immediate phenomenon in late-1990s Korean PC bangs.

links.took: Playfully macabre undead-kingdom knight action packed with crumbling graveyards, pumpkin monsters, and gallows humor.
links.added: Brought tongue-in-cheek gothic hack-and-slash into 3D PlayStation adventure with skeletal hero Sir Daniel Fortesque, detachable arm attacks, and Tim Burton-inspired art.
links.extra: Developed by SCE Cambridge Studio, originally pitched as a 3D fusion of Ghosts 'n Goblins and The Nightmare Before Christmas.

links.took: Turn-based elemental type matchups, four-move creature kits, and custom-trained Game Boy monster rosters.
links.added: Brought all 151 original Pokémon into animated 3D Nintendo 64 arena battles with Transfer Pak cartridge import, lively announcer commentary, and four-player minigames.
links.extra: First global home-console showcase letting players see their handheld Pokémon teams clash in 3D.

links.took: Bullfrog's terrain-sculpting divine spells, tribal follower growth, and apocalyptic god-game warfare.
links.added: Moved the action onto a seamlessly rotatable 3D globe with direct RTS troop commands and a mortal spellcasting Shaman leading the tribe on the ground.
links.extra: Bullfrog's first Populous developed after Peter Molyneux's departure, blending classic god-game spectacle with modern 3D RTS.

links.took: High-speed arcade powerslide drifting, sun-drenched seaside circuits, and upbeat electronic racing energy.
links.added: Paired stylish Gouraud-shaded visuals and an acid-jazz soundtrack with a branching Grand Prix team career unlocking 320 distinctive cars.
links.extra: Widely praised as the aesthetic and mechanical apex of the original PlayStation Ridge Racer era.

links.took: tri-Ace's real-time action JRPG battles, Private Action character skits, and intricate skill-driven Item Creation.
links.added: Introduced dual playable protagonists Claude and Rena on PlayStation with full 3D battlefields, sprawling crafting loops, and 86 distinct character endings.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Ocean: The Second Story

links.extra: Became tri-Ace's breakout international PlayStation classic and template for its subsequent RPGs.

links.took: Cockpit-driven Star Wars starfighter dogfighting, Rebel Alliance squadron missions, and classic trilogy spacecraft.
links.added: Distilled flight-sim keyboard complexity into fast, approachable planetary surface-attack arcade action powered by Factor 5's custom N64 microcode.

src.t: Time Extension, Julian Eggebrecht Factor 5 retrospective; Wikipedia: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron

links.extra: Factor 5 built Rogue Squadron from its canceled Return to Fractalus prototype rather than Shadows of the Empire, creating a beloved N64 hit.

links.took: Fast planetary starfighter combat, wingman commands, and gold-medal mastery objectives across classic trilogy worlds.
links.added: Leapt to GameCube launch hardware with film-quality Battle of Yavin and Endor space armadas, volumetric clouds, and dazzling 60fps lighting.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader

links.extra: Factor 5 directly evolved its N64 Rogue Squadron template into GameCube's defining technical launch showpiece.

links.took: Capcom's anime-styled Alpha engine, air blocking, Alpha Counters, and multi-tiered Super Combo meter play.
links.added: Introduced three selectable fighting styles (A-ISM, V-ISM, X-ISM), Guard Crush meters, a massive 30+ fighter roster, and a console RPG-like World Tour mode.
links.extra: Stood as Capcom's most content-packed 2D Street Fighter package of the late 1990s.

links.took: The concept of a dedicated single-player World Tour mode blending fighting-game matches with RPG stat leveling and globe-trotting challenges.
links.added: Expanded Alpha 3's menu-based World Tour into a full 3D open-district action-RPG adventure where custom avatars train under iconic World Warriors.

src.t: Game Informer / Siliconera, Takayuki Nakayama Street Fighter 6 interviews; Wikipedia: Street Fighter Alpha 3

links.extra: Street Fighter 6 director Takayuki Nakayama revived the World Tour name and RPG-progression spirit first pioneered in Alpha 3.

links.took: Sega AM1's rapid-fire zombie light-gun shooting, locational limb dismemberment, and weak-point boss dossiers.
links.added: Moved onto Dreamcast-class NAOMI arcade visuals with richer civilian-rescue branching paths, a sprawling Venetian outbreak, and famously quotable B-movie voice acting.

src.t: Wikipedia: The House of the Dead 2

links.extra: Also spawned Sega's cult edutainment spinoff The Typing of the Dead using the exact same engine and stages.

links.took: SNK's three-on-three crossover team fighting pitting Fatal Fury, Art of Fighting, Ikari, and original heroes together.
links.added: Distilled four years of Neo Geo iteration into a tightly balanced non-canon 'Dream Match' featuring 38 fighters, custom team editing, and dual Advanced and Extra playstyles.
links.extra: Universally revered alongside Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike as a golden-age competitive 2D fighting benchmark.

links.took: The 4X fantasy strategy template uniting Civilization-style empire expansion, spellbooks, and hero-led turn-based tactical battles.
links.added: Brought detailed hand-drawn isometric overland maps, 12 distinct fantasy races, simultaneous multiplayer turns, and siege warfare to Triumph Studios' long-running series.

src.t: Lennart Sas (Triumph Studios) retrospective interviews; Wikipedia: Age of Wonders

links.extra: Triumph co-founder Lennart Sas repeatedly cited SimTex's Master of Magic as the primary conceptual inspiration behind Age of Wonders.

links.took: Indirectly steering streams of single-minded marching critters past lethal hazards to safety using limited directional orders.
links.added: Turned directional arrow placement into a frantic four-player arena sport—steering mice into your rocket while redirecting cats into rivals—as the first online multiplayer console game.
links.extra: Built by Sonic Team under Yuji Naka to stress-test Sega Dreamcast's built-in modem before Phantasy Star Online.

links.took: Seasonal crop planting, livestock care, town festivals, and courtship life-simulation loops.
links.added: Refined the formula on PlayStation with richer Mineral Town villager schedules, cooking recipes, mine exploration, and a three-year farm restoration arc.

src.t: Wikipedia: Harvest Moon: Back to Nature

links.extra: Its cast and Mineral Town layout became the enduring canonical template of classic Harvest Moon.

links.took: The cozy seasonal rhythm of rebuilding an inherited farm, befriending Mineral Town villagers, mining, and attending seasonal festivals.
links.added: Expanded the blueprint onto PC with open-ended play, deep artisan crafting chains, combat-filled mines, customizable farm layouts, and co-op multiplayer.

src.t: PC Gamer & Game Developer, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe) interviews; Wikipedia: Stardew Valley

links.extra: Eric Barone routinely named Harvest Moon: Back to Nature his favorite entry in the series and primary blueprint for Stardew Valley.

links.took: Koichi Ishii's real-time action-RPG swordplay, elemental spirits, and lush storybook Mana world.
links.added: Reinvented progression with hand-painted watercolor 2D PlayStation art, non-linear vignette quests, pet raising, and a Land Make grid where players place lands onto the map.
links.extra: Directed by series creator Koichi Ishii with Yoko Shimomura's acclaimed orchestral soundtrack.

links.took: High-speed arcade street driving with aggressive police pursuits and traffic-dodging chases.
links.added: Broke completely free of closed tracks by dropping players into a living, open-world 3D Chicago with free-route checkpoint racing and realistic city traffic.
links.extra: Angel Studios' 1999 PC hit caught Rockstar Games' attention and sparked the studio's evolution into Rockstar San Diego.

links.took: Angel Studios' Angel Game Engine (AGE) open-city driving physics, free-route checkpoint navigation, and lively urban traffic.
links.added: Shifted from daytime Chicago sightseeing into nocturnal underground street-racing tournaments across open-world New York and London for PlayStation 2's launch.

src.t: Wikipedia: Midtown Madness; Midnight Club: Street Racing

links.extra: Sam Houser's love for Angel Studios' Midtown Madness directly led Rockstar to commission Midnight Club and later acquire the studio.

links.took: Third-person 3D exploration, athletic traversing, and action-adventure puzzle discovery across exotic ruins.
links.added: Pioneered a truly open-world 3D voxel alien planet (Adelpha) with non-linear region order, reactive native faction reputation, dynamic AI routines, and a live Moscow Symphony score.
links.extra: Developed by Belgian studio Appeal, anticipating modern open-world action-adventure structure years ahead of its time.

links.took: An open 3D action-adventure world populated by reactive townsfolk, non-linear mission zones, and emergent stealth-action traversal.
links.added: Unified open-city exploration with fluid parkour climbing, social-crowd blending, and synchronized vantage-point map discovery.
links.extra: Retrospectives widely credit Outcast as a trailblazing blueprint for modern 3D open-world action-adventures.

links.took: Capcom's kinetic brawling DNA built around grabbing scattered weapons, throwing furniture, and brawling across interactive set-pieces.
links.added: Fused environmental brawling with free-roaming 3D arena fighting where collecting three Power Stones triggers explosive super-powered transformations.
links.extra: Capcom's beloved NAOMI and Dreamcast original became a cult template for 3D arena brawlers.

links.took: Call-and-response musical rhythm timing paired with eccentric cartoon storytelling.
links.added: Reframed rhythm inputs as directional dance moves and ray-gun blasts during a live retro-futuristic alien-invasion broadcast starring reporter Ulala.
links.extra: Created by Tetsuya Mizuguchi's United Game Artists as one of the Dreamcast's signature stylish originals.

links.took: Tetsuya Mizuguchi and United Game Artists' vision of binding visual spectacle, controller feedback, and interactive electronic beats into one groove.
links.added: Abstracted campy dance battles into a hypnotic synesthetic wireframe rail shooter where every lock-on shot composes layers of the pulsing trance soundtrack.
links.extra: Both Dreamcast classics flowed straight from Mizuguchi's United Game Artists studio at Sega.

links.took: Multi-disc PlayStation cinematic JRPG scale with pre-rendered painterly backgrounds, FMV spectacles, and dramatic party storytelling.
links.added: Distinguished turn-based battles through timed button-press 'Addition' attack combos and winged elemental Dragoon transformations.
links.extra: Sony Computer Entertainment Japan's ambitious internal answer to Square's Final Fantasy VII juggernaut.

links.took: Sega AM3's ultra-responsive arcade pick-up-and-play feel, crisp 60fps presentation, and tight risk-reward timing.
links.added: Applied that instant arcade polish to tennis with intuitive two-button topspin and lob mechanics, dive volleys, and an addictive World Tour minigame career.
links.extra: Developed by Sega AM3 (soon renamed Hitmaker), redefining arcade sports accessibility on NAOMI and Dreamcast.

links.took: Demonstrated how radically simplified, timing-based arcade tennis controls could hook non-gamers and veterans alike in seconds.
links.added: Replaced controller buttons and manual court movement entirely with intuitive Wii Remote motion swings for instant living-room multiplayer.
links.extra: Virtua Tennis set the modern benchmark for hyper-accessible arcade tennis.

links.took: id Tech 3's crisp 3D architecture, smooth curved surfaces, and nimble kinetic movement from former id Software designer American McGee.
links.added: Reimagined Lewis Carroll's Wonderland as a macabre psychological gothic third-person action-adventure armed with Vorpal Blades and Playing Cards.
links.extra: Developed by Rogue Entertainment and published by EA with Chris Vrenna's haunting music-box industrial score.

links.took: Capcom's iconic Street Fighter fundamentals, iconic World Warriors, and precise arcade spacing.
links.added: United historic arcade rivals Capcom and SNK in one crossover fighter using a four-point Ratio team-building system and selectable Capcom or SNK Grooves.

src.t: Wikipedia: Capcom vs. SNK: Millennium Fight 2000

links.extra: Fulfilled a decade-long arcade dream by pitting Ryu and Chun-Li directly against Kyo, Iori, Terry, and Mai.

links.took: Selectable ISM meter systems letting players choose how their fighters build and spend super energy.
links.added: Evolved ISM selection into distinct Capcom-style (3-level Super) and SNK-style (chargeable desperation) Grooves bridging both companies' fighting philosophies.

src.t: Wikipedia: Capcom vs. SNK: Millennium Fight 2000

links.extra: Directly carried Alpha 3's selectable-system experimentation into the Capcom vs. SNK line.

links.took: SNK's star-studded roster, team-order strategy, and Extra/Advanced meter dichotomy.
links.added: Redrew SNK legends in Capcom's NAOMI sprite style and integrated SNK Groove power-charging alongside Capcom's four-button attack layout.

src.t: Wikipedia: Capcom vs. SNK: Millennium Fight 2000

links.extra: SNK's competitive KOF '98 legacy supplied half the DNA of this landmark cross-company collaboration.

links.took: Heartbeat's deep multi-tier Vocation class mastery and parallel-world Dragon Quest storytelling.
links.added: Moved the series onto PlayStation 3D rotatable environments with monster vocations and a sprawling 100-hour quest restoring vanished islands one tablet at a time.
links.extra: Became the best-selling PlayStation game in Japan, shipping over four million copies.

links.took: Long-form episodic town storytelling and the leap into 3D polygonal Dragon Quest exploration.
links.added: Replaced 2D sprites on rotatable 3D backgrounds with Level-5's seamless cel-shaded PlayStation 2 world, voice acting, and full-scale overworld adventuring.
links.extra: Dragon Quest VII proved the series' PlayStation transition before Level-5 modernized it for global audiences in VIII.

links.took: Reflections' 1970s cinema car-chase physics, suspension body roll, and open-city PlayStation missions.
links.added: Introduced curved roads, four sprawling international cities, and the landmark ability to exit vehicles on foot to commandeer other cars in 3D.
links.extra: Allowed players to step out of cars in open 3D cities nearly a full year before Grand Theft Auto III.

links.took: Demonstrated the thrill of seamlessly switching between on-foot exploration and carjacking inside living 3D PlayStation cities.
links.added: Unleashed unrestricted criminal sandbox freedom with full third-person gunplay, emergent police escalations, and non-linear mission design on PlayStation 2.

src.t: Wikipedia: Driver 2; Grand Theft Auto III

links.extra: Driver 2's on-foot vehicle-swapping bridged 1999's driving sandboxes to GTA III's full open-world revolution.

links.took: Neon-soaked nocturnal illegal street racing through traffic-packed urban shortcuts.
links.added: Fused midnight tuner culture with deep aftermarket visual customization, drag and drift events, and licensed import cars.

src.t: Wikipedia: Midnight Club: Street Racing; Need for Speed: Underground

links.extra: Midnight Club proved the commercial power of late-night urban street racing three years before NFS Underground.

links.took: Angel Studios' Angel Game Engine (AGE) open-city streaming and realistic vehicle-handling framework built for PlayStation 2.
links.added: Evolved after Take-Two's acquisition of Angel Studios (becoming Rockstar San Diego) into the proprietary RAGE engine powering GTA IV's physics-rich Liberty City.

src.t: Wikipedia: Rockstar San Diego; Rockstar Advanced Game Engine

links.extra: Angel Studios' Midtown Madness and Midnight Club engine lineage directly became Rockstar's flagship RAGE tech.

links.took: Johto and Kanto's 251-creature adventure, real-time day-night cycle, and Pokémon breeding.
links.added: Introduced animated battle sprites, a dedicated Suicune subplot, the endgame Battle Tower, and the franchise's first selectable female protagonist (Kris).
links.extra: Also pioneered Japan's Mobile System GB cell-phone adapter for online trading and battles in 2000.

links.took: Wario's greedy treasure-hunting platformer identity and physical enemy-battering moveset.
links.added: Made Wario completely invincible—turning enemy attacks like fire, flat-squashing, and zombie bites into puzzle-solving transformations across an interconnected day-and-night world.
links.extra: Nintendo R&D1 refined Wario Land II's no-death puzzle-platforming into a Metroidvania-like Game Boy Color masterpiece.

links.took: Status-effect puzzle transformations (Flaming, Zombie, Flat, Bouncy Wario) and treasure-focused stage secrets.
links.added: Reintroduced a health bar alongside explosive Frog Switch escape sprints back to the portal on Game Boy Advance.
links.extra: Carried over R&D1's beloved transformation puzzle mechanics while tightening pace for GBA.

links.took: Pyro Studios' real-time isometric WWII stealth tactics built around enemy vision cones and specialized squad roles.
links.added: Added rotatable 3D building interiors, swappable enemy uniform disguises, inventory looting, a thief and dog specialist, and wide-open sandbox infiltration.
links.extra: Universally hailed as the pinnacle of classic real-time stealth-tactics design.

links.took: Complex multi-specialist real-time stealth puzzles built on overlapping vision cones, disguises, and environmental accidents.
links.added: Modernized classic Commandos-era stealth tactics with Showdown Mode synchronized pause-planning and crisp visual sightline tools.

src.t: Wikipedia: Commandos 2: Men of Courage; Desperados III

links.extra: Mimimi Games' modern real-time tactics revival directly built on the sandbox standard set by Commandos 2.

links.took: Historically grounded WWII combat flight simulation blending authentic aircraft performance with campaign missions.
links.added: Set a new benchmark for Eastern Front aerial realism with detailed aerodynamic stalls, engine management, component-level damage models, and multiplayer dogfighting.
links.extra: Oleg Maddox's Moscow studio revitalized hardcore PC WWII combat flight sims for the 21st century.

links.took: Flat Mode-7-style circuit drifting, coin-boost top speed, and tight retro kart handling.
links.added: Delivered the first handheld Mario Kart on Game Boy Advance with 20 new courses, single-cartridge link multiplayer, and all 20 original SNES tracks unlockable.
links.extra: Developed by Intelligent Systems, pioneering the tradition of including retro classic cups in Mario Kart.

links.took: Rule-bending arcade basketball built around high-flying dunks, momentum streaks, and larger-than-life athleticism.
links.added: Reinvented arcade hoops in 3D three-on-three asphalt playgrounds with Trick Stick ankle-breaking dribble combos and game-swinging Gamebreaker dunks.
links.extra: Launched EA Sports BIG's wildly popular arcade sports sub-label alongside SSX.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's immersive daily-schedule life simulation, Virtua Fighter-derived street brawling, and cinematic Quick Time Events.
links.added: Expanded Ryo Hazuki's revenge quest from quiet Yokosuka across dense multi-story Hong Kong districts, Kowloon's Walled City, and serene rural Guilin.
links.extra: Introduced time-skipping convenience and grander open-district exploration on Dreamcast and Xbox.

links.took: Ryo and Shenhua's cliffhanger journey into Guilin's Bailu Village along with daily routines, part-time jobs, and martial-arts training.
links.added: Resumed the story 18 years later via Kickstarter on Unreal Engine 4 with stamina-driven training loops and expanded Chinese village exploration.
links.extra: Directly picked up the narrative from the exact cave cliffhanger ending of Shenmue II.

links.took: Bullfrog veterans' wry British corporate satire, whimsical alien-style visitor ailments, and buoyant economic room management.
links.added: Built a curved, rotatable three-deck toroidal space station where ex-Bullfrog studio Mucky Foot balanced shopping plazas, alien tourists, and terraformed bio-decks.
links.extra: Founded by ex-Bullfrog developers including Gary Carr, Finbarr Flynn, and Guy Simmons after EA's acquisition.

links.took: Tactile god-hand creature pickup, territorial room-claiming, and autonomous alien/monster workers managed indirectly.
links.added: Shifted from dark underground lair defense to a colorful hitchhiker's-guide sci-fi starbase with nine distinct alien species and floating AI overseer VAL.
links.extra: Critics and fans embraced Startopia as the true spiritual fusion of Theme Hospital and Dungeon Keeper.

links.took: Compact top-down Game Boy dungeon-crawling, two-item button swapping, and charming handheld Zelda sprite craftsmanship.
links.added: Built intricate time-traveling past-and-present overworld puzzles with the Harp of Ages and cross-game password secrets linking directly to Oracle of Seasons.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Seasons and Oracle of Ages

links.extra: Directed by Hidemaro Fujibayashi at Capcom's Flagship studio under Nintendo supervision.

links.took: Hidemaro Fujibayashi and Flagship's inventive dual-state world puzzles and rich side-quest collectibles.
links.added: Swapped Game Boy Color time-shifting for Game Boy Advance size-shrinking into miniature Minish realms alongside Kinstone map-unlocking fusion.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap

links.extra: Fujibayashi went on from the Oracle games and Minish Cap to direct Skyward Sword, Breath of the Wild, and Tears of the Kingdom.

links.took: David Jaffe and SingleTrac's chaotic free-for-all arena car combat with character-specific special weapons.
links.added: Rebooted the series on PlayStation 2 with 60fps destructible urban arenas, brutal vehicular speed, and grimdark psychological horror backstories.
links.extra: Created by Incognito Entertainment (founded by former SingleTrac developers) and widely hailed as the series' peak.

links.took: Sega AM2's razor-sharp three-button martial-arts fundamentals, frame-advantage depth, and flat-arena ring-out discipline.
links.added: Pioneered VF.NET magnetic player-card arcade rankings, adaptive AI ghosts trained on top players, and an industry-leading console tutorial mode.
links.extra: Re-energized competitive 3D fighting on NAOMI 2 and PlayStation 2 with deep training tools.

links.took: Hideo Kojima's cinematic anime storytelling, Yoji Shinkawa's angular mechanical design, and dramatic codec-style presentation.
links.added: Traded tactical espionage for blazing 60fps PlayStation 2 zero-gravity Orbital Frame aerial combat, homing laser swarms, and melee blade dashing.

src.t: Wikipedia: Zone of the Enders (video game)

links.extra: Produced by Hideo Kojima and directed by Noriaki Okamura; notably bundled with the eagerly awaited Metal Gear Solid 2 demo.

links.took: High-speed 3D lock-on mecha dueling driven by rapid directional dashing and sweeping energy projectiles.
links.added: Expanded arena skirmishes into a story-driven 3D action adventure with free vertical flight, enemy grabbing, and sweeping cinematic camera locks.

src.t: Wikipedia: Zone of the Enders (video game)

links.extra: Translated Sega's fast-paced anime-mecha duel feel into a sleek single-player PS2 action showcase.

links.took: Lethal, slow-paced tactical squad shooting where realistic ballistics, weapon jamming, and communication outweigh lone-wolf reflexes.
links.added: Delivered an official free-to-play U.S. Army Unreal Engine 2 recruitment shooter gating online roles behind mandatory basic-training and medic certification drills.
links.extra: Created by the MOVES Institute as a groundbreaking free-to-play PC tactical shooter and government recruitment experiment.

links.took: Criterion's perilous oncoming-traffic near-misses, boost gauges, and dramatic slow-motion crash replays.
links.added: Debuted the iconic puzzle-destruction Crash Mode, chainable Burnout boosts, and slicker 60fps arcade drifting physics.
links.extra: Crash Mode instantly became one of the most beloved party modes of the PlayStation 2, GameCube, and Xbox generation.

links.took: Chainable Burnout boosts, ultra-responsive high-speed drift physics, and intersection-wrecking Crash Mode puzzles.
links.added: Turned rivals into targets with aggressive Takedown shunts, Aftertouch mid-air crash steering, and Crashbreaker explosions.
links.extra: Criterion built directly on Burnout 2's handling and Crash Mode to craft its all-time arcade racing classic.

links.took: Westwood's iconic GDI vs. Nod Tiberium War units, Obelisks of Light, Mammoth Tanks, and base structures.
links.added: Dropped players down to eye level as Commando Havoc in a first- and third-person shooter whose multiplayer 'C&C Mode' let teams drive vehicles and destroy enemy RTS base interiors.
links.extra: Westwood's sole FPS pioneered team-based asymmetrical RTS-structure destruction years before Battlefield-era base assaults.

links.took: Level-5's blend of Zelda-inspired 3D dungeon crawling, upgradeable weapons, and Georama town reconstruction.
links.added: Upgraded to lush cel-shaded visuals (released as Dark Cloud 2 in North America) with invention photography, a customizable Ridepod mech, Spheda golf, and dual time-traveling leads.
links.extra: Widely acclaimed as one of the PlayStation 2's richest, most feature-packed action-RPGs.

links.took: Level-5's luminous PlayStation 2 cel-shading pipeline, expressive animation craft, and warm storybook RPG atmosphere.
links.added: Applied that visual mastery to Akira Toriyama's artwork across an expansive seamless 3D overworld with classic turn-based Dragon Quest pacing.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dark Chronicle; Dragon Quest VIII

links.extra: Level-5's cel-shaded triumph in Dark Chronicle directly paved the way for Square Enix entrusting them with Dragon Quest VIII.

links.took: Click-driven real-time loot hunting, dark dungeon crawling, and addictive gear-upgrade momentum.
links.added: Eliminated loading screens entirely across a continuous 3D fantasy continent navigated by an eight-member automated party and loot-carrying pack mule.
links.extra: Designed by Chris Taylor's Gas Powered Games after Total Annihilation, showcasing seamless 3D world streaming.

links.took: Daisuke Ishiwatari's heavy-metal anime aesthetic, high-mobility air dashing, and eccentric character toolkits.
links.added: Cemented the modern anime fighting-game template with combo-escaping Psych Bursts, sharpened Roman Cancels, and ultra-crisp high-resolution sprite animation.
links.extra: Known as Guilty Gear X2 in North America, its revisions anchored competitive air-dasher tournaments for a decade.

links.took: Arc System Works' hyper-kinetic air-dasher physics, Roman-style cancels, Burst escapes, and wildly asymmetric character gimmicks.
links.added: Moved onto widescreen HD sprites with a dedicated 'Drive' button giving every fighter a signature unique mechanic and an episodic visual-novel story mode.
links.extra: Toshimichi Mori created BlazBlue at Arc System Works as a spiritual successor while Sega temporarily held Guilty Gear rights.

links.took: Smilebit's cel-shaded Tokyo-to inline skating, rail grinding, graffiti tagging, and eclectic funk-hip-hop soundtrack.
links.added: Removed strict stage timers and analog-stick spray inputs on Xbox for uninterrupted, interconnected open-district trick flow and higher-speed rail combos.
links.extra: Became an iconic Xbox bundle title and cult favorite for its seamless flow and Hideki Naganuma beats.

links.took: Timer-free open-city cel-shaded rail grinding, trick chaining, rival turf wars, and Hideki Naganuma's funky breakbeat energy.
links.added: Expanded movement with inline skates, skateboards, BMX bikes, boost packs, and modern combo-multiplier graffiti battles.

src.t: Wikipedia: Jet Set Radio Future; Bomb Rush Cyberfunk

links.extra: Team Reptile directly channeled JSRF's flow-first open districts and enlisted composer Hideki Naganuma.

links.took: Cinematic WWII espionage-and-frontline FPS pacing, historical authenticity, and Michael Giacchino's stirring orchestral score.
links.added: Brought an unforgettable Omaha Beach D-Day storming and Operation Market Garden campaign to PlayStation 2, GameCube, and Xbox.
links.extra: EA Los Angeles' multi-million-selling console hit cemented cinematic WWII shooters on sixth-generation hardware.

links.took: Creative Assembly's signature marriage of Risk-like turn-based campaign provinces and massive real-time 3D battlefield clashes.
links.added: Broadened the theater across medieval Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East with stone castle sieges, papal excommunication, Crusades, and royal princess diplomacy.
links.extra: Proved Total War's formula could span centuries and continents far beyond feudal Japan.

links.took: Feudal European grand conquest, Crusades and Jihads, papal politics, and multi-layered castle siege warfare.
links.added: Upgraded to Rome: Total War's free-roaming 3D campaign map, individualized soldier armor models, gunpowder eras, and New World voyages.
links.extra: Directly carried Medieval's beloved historical systems into Creative Assembly's full-3D campaign era.

links.took: High-speed wall-jumping, dash-canceling, and cybernetic Reploid action from Capcom's X timeline.
links.added: Inti Creates shifted focus to razor-sharp Z-Saber melee combat, interconnected mission hubs, strict performance grading, and sacrifice-based Cyber-Elf upgrades on GBA.
links.extra: Launched Inti Creates' acclaimed four-game Game Boy Advance saga set a century after Mega Man X.

links.took: Monolith's witty 1960s spy-parody tone, Cate Archer's espionage gadgets, and blend of stealth with punchy FPS gunplay.
links.added: Introduced Lithtech Jupiter graphics, RPG-style skill-point upgrades, cooperative missions, and unforgettable set-pieces like dueling ninjas inside an airborne trailer home.

src.t: Wikipedia: No One Lives Forever 2: A Spy in H.A.R.M.'s Way

links.extra: Critically acclaimed sequel that pushed Monolith's Lithtech tech before F.E.A.R.

links.took: Persistent open-world online community spaces, player-run vendor markets, and freeform character stat builds.
links.added: Blended charming 2D anime sprites over rotatable 3D worlds with branching job trees, monster-card gear slotting, and weekly War of Emperium guild sieges.
links.extra: Developed by Gravity in South Korea, becoming a massive global anime-styled MMORPG phenomenon.

links.took: South Korea's thriving PC bang online RPG ecosystem, brisk click-driven combat, and guild-versus-guild castle siege warfare.
links.added: Replaced Lineage's grim Western-fantasy tone with bright Norse-inspired manhwa art, social emote culture, and collectible monster-card customization.
links.extra: Broadened Korean MMORPG appeal globally across Southeast Asia, Japan, Europe, and the Americas.

links.took: Fixed-camera pre-rendered survival horror, tank controls, ink-ribbon saves, and tense Umbrella mansion mystery.
links.added: Removed magical Item Boxes in favor of dropping gear directly on the floor and debuted live 'Partner Zapping' between Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen aboard the Ecliptic Express.
links.extra: Final mainline entry built in Capcom's classic fixed-camera survival horror template before Resident Evil 4.

links.took: Firefly Studios' tactile castle-wall construction, peasant food-and-tax economy, and boiling-oil siege defense.
links.added: Shifted to arid desert oasis maps where fertile farmland is fiercely contested, adding Arab mercenary troops, fire ballistae, and 50-mission Skirmish Trails.
links.extra: Endured for over two decades as the fan-favorite standalone entry in the Stronghold franchise.

links.took: Nintendo's quintessential top-down 16-bit action-adventure dungeon craft, swordplay, and puzzle tools.
links.added: Paired the SNES classic on Game Boy Advance with Flagship's brand-new Four Swords—debuting four-player link-cable co-op-and-competitive Zelda dungeon raiding.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past and Four Swords

links.extra: Four Swords launched Zelda's multiplayer lineage, directly leading to Four Swords Adventures and Tri Force Heroes.
